before: Despite being harder to quantify, pain and suffering damages are often the largest component of a personal injury settlement or verdict. For an overview of how non-economic damages fit into the broader landscape of injury compensation, see Cornell Law Institute's legal definition of damages.
after: For an overview of how non-economic damages fit into the broader landscape of injury compensation, see the Legal Information Institute at Cornell Law School's legal definition of damages.

before: Neither Georgia nor South Carolina law sets a formula for calculating pain and suffering. Instead, insurance adjusters, attorneys, and juries use several accepted methods to arrive at a number that reflects the severity of what you have endured.
after: Neither Georgia nor South Carolina law sets a formula for calculating pain and suffering. Instead, insurance adjusters and attorneys use a few informal conventions to put a number on it in negotiation. Neither is a rule of law, and a jury is never bound by them.

before:
The most widely used approach. Your total economic damages (medical bills, lost wages, property damage, and other out-of-pocket costs) are multiplied by a factor — typically between 1.5 and 5 — to estimate the value of your non-economic losses.

The multiplier increases based on injury severity:

  • 1.5 – 2× — minor injuries with full recovery (soft tissue, minor whiplash)
  • 2 – 3× — moderate injuries requiring extended treatment (herniated discs, fractures)
  • 3 – 4× — serious injuries with lasting effects (multiple surgeries, partial disability)
  • 4 – 5× or higher — catastrophic or permanent injuries (traumatic brain injuries, spinal cord injuries, amputation)

Example: If your economic damages total $80,000 and a multiplier of 3 is applied, your pain and suffering would be valued at $240,000, bringing the total claim to $320,000.
after:
Your total economic damages (medical bills, lost wages, property damage, and other out-of-pocket costs) are multiplied by a factor to estimate the value of your non-economic losses. The factor rises with the severity and permanence of the injury, from a minor soft-tissue strain to a traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury or amputation. It is a negotiating convention, not a rule of law.

Purely hypothetical example: If your economic damages total $80,000 and a multiplier of 3 is applied, your pain and suffering would be valued at $240,000, bringing the total claim to $320,000.

before:
This approach assigns a daily dollar amount to your pain and suffering and multiplies it by the number of days you are expected to be affected. The daily rate is often tied to your actual daily earnings, on the theory that your suffering each day is worth at least as much as your daily wage.

Example: If you earn $200 per day and your recovery period is 365 days, the per diem calculation yields $73,000 in pain and suffering damages.

before: If your case goes to trial, the jury has broad discretion to award whatever amount it believes fairly compensates you for your pain and suffering. Jurors consider the evidence, the severity of injuries, the credibility of testimony, and their own sense of fairness. This is why presenting a compelling, well-documented case is critical.
after: If your case goes to trial, the jury has broad discretion to award whatever amount it believes fairly compensates you for your pain and suffering. Jurors consider the evidence, the severity of injuries, the credibility of testimony, and their own sense of fairness. In Georgia the legal measure is the "enlightened conscience of an impartial jury" (O.C.G.A. § 9-10-184). Since Georgia's 2025 tort-reform act (SB 68), lawyers may suggest a dollar figure for pain and suffering only in closing argument, and only if it is rationally tied to the evidence; either side may also ask for a phased trial in which the jury decides fault before hearing about damages (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-15). This is why presenting a compelling, well-documented case is critical.

before: No cap on pain and suffering in most personal injury cases. Georgia does not limit non-economic damages in car accidents, truck accidents, premises liability, or other general negligence claims. However, Georgia previously had a cap on non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases, which was struck down as unconstitutional by the Georgia Supreme Court in Atlanta Oculoplastic Surgery, P.C. v. Nestlehutt (2010). As a result, there is currently no cap on pain and suffering in any personal injury case in Georgia.
after: No cap on pain and suffering in most personal injury cases. Georgia does not limit non-economic damages in car accidents, truck accidents, premises liability, or other general negligence claims. However, Georgia previously had a cap on non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases, which was struck down as unconstitutional by the Georgia Supreme Court in Atlanta Oculoplastic Surgery, P.C. v. Nestlehutt, 286 Ga. 731 (2010). As a result, Georgia has no cap on pain and suffering in ordinary negligence cases, including medical malpractice. The one common exception is a claim against the State of Georgia itself, where the Tort Claims Act caps all damages at $1 million per person (O.C.G.A. § 50-21-29).

before:
No general cap on pain and suffering in most personal injury cases. South Carolina does not limit non-economic damages in car accident, truck accident, or premises liability cases. However, South Carolina does cap non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases at $350,000 per defendant and $1.05 million total regardless of the number of defendants (S.C. Code § 15-32-220).

Outside of medical malpractice, juries in both states have the freedom to award whatever amount they believe is fair based on the evidence presented.
after:
No general cap on pain and suffering in most personal injury cases. South Carolina does not limit non-economic damages in car accident, truck accident, or premises liability cases. However, South Carolina does cap non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases. The statute sets the limit at $350,000 per health care provider or facility and $1.05 million for all of them together, per injured person, and indexes it to inflation each year — for 2026 the figures are $596,001 and $1,788,002 (S.C. Code § 15-32-220; S.C. Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Office). The cap falls away if the provider was grossly negligent, wilful, wanton or reckless, or committed fraud or altered records, and it never limits economic damages. Claims against a South Carolina government entity are capped at $300,000 per person under the Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-120).

Outside of South Carolina medical malpractice claims and claims against a government entity, juries in both states decide the amount on the evidence, with no statutory ceiling.

before:
Pain and suffering damages are available in virtually every personal injury case where negligence caused physical or emotional harm. The types of cases that most frequently produce significant pain and suffering awards include:

  • Car accidents — the most common source of personal injury claims, ranging from minor whiplash to catastrophic injuries
  • Truck accidents — collisions with commercial vehicles often cause severe, life-altering injuries due to the size disparity
  • Motorcycle accidents — riders lack the protection of an enclosed vehicle, resulting in higher rates of serious injury
  • Pedestrian accidents — pedestrians struck by vehicles suffer some of the most severe injuries
  • Slip and fall injuries — falls can cause broken bones, head injuries, and chronic back pain, especially for older adults
  • Medical malpractice — surgical errors, misdiagnosis, and medication mistakes can cause prolonged suffering
  • Wrongful death — surviving family members can recover for their own pain and suffering from the loss of a loved one
  • Dog bites — attacks often cause scarring, disfigurement, and lasting psychological trauma
  • Nursing home abuse — elderly victims of neglect or abuse suffer significant physical and emotional harm
  • Premises liability — injuries on unsafe property due to a property owner's negligence
  • Product liability — defective products that cause injury, including burns, lacerations, or toxic exposure

Pain and suffering damages are available in virtually every personal injury case where negligence caused a physical injury — and the mental suffering that comes with it. The types of cases that most frequently produce significant pain and suffering awards include:

  • Car accidents — the most common source of personal injury claims, ranging from minor whiplash to catastrophic injuries
  • Truck accidents — collisions with commercial vehicles often cause severe, life-altering injuries due to the size disparity
  • Motorcycle accidents — riders lack the protection of an enclosed vehicle, resulting in higher rates of serious injury
  • Pedestrian accidents — pedestrians struck by vehicles suffer some of the most severe injuries
  • Slip and fall injuries — falls can cause broken bones, head injuries, and chronic back pain, especially for older adults
  • Medical malpractice — surgical errors, misdiagnosis, and medication mistakes can cause prolonged suffering
  • Wrongful death — in South Carolina the family recovers for its own grief, mental shock and loss of companionship (S.C. Code § 15-51-40); in Georgia the claim is measured by the full value of the decedent's life, and the decedent's own pain and suffering before death is recovered by the estate (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-1)
  • Dog bites — attacks often cause scarring, disfigurement, and lasting psychological trauma
  • Nursing home abuse — elderly victims of neglect or abuse suffer significant physical and emotional harm
  • Premises liability — injuries on unsafe property due to a property owner's negligence
  • Product liability — defective products that cause injury, including burns, lacerations, or toxic exposure

before: Pain and suffering damages compensate injury victims for physical discomfort, emotional distress, anxiety, and diminished quality of life beyond economic losses. Insurers use multiplier or per diem methods to calculate these non-economic damages. Georgia does not cap pain and suffering in most personal injury cases, and South Carolina likewise imposes no general cap. Comparative fault reduces awards proportionally in both states, barring recovery at 50% fault in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) and 51% in South Carolina.

before: Pain and suffering refers to the physical pain and emotional distress you experience as a result of an injury caused by someone else's negligence. It is a category of non-economic damages that compensates for losses like chronic pain, anxiety, depression, loss of enjoyment of life, and loss of consortium — things that do not have a specific dollar amount attached to them.
